5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Taholah Washington, Jan 21 1920 Sup't Cushman Indian School Tacoma Washington. Dear Sir, The Fee Patents arrived that you kindly forwarded yesterday after letter mailed to you. Delayed somewhere on the way. The mail delivery to this station seems to rest quite frequently, as far as Moclips station is concerned, upon the discretion of the Postmaster. I would advise that when Hattie Major was home Christmas Holidays she made application to this office for money due her on deposit here. The Chief clerk being absent for a week I did not look the matter up until his return. I advanced her personally $5,00 at the time. Would you please advise her that there are no funds on deposit here to her credit, that the estate from which she will when settled receive funds is not as yet settled and so we are unable to advance her $25,00 as requested. Respectfully, [signature] Eugene W. Niss Superintendent. EWH/MM 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Mora, Washington. May 8, 1920. Special Supervisor in Charge Cushman Indian School. Tacoma, Washington. Dear Sir: Herewith enclosed twelve dollars ($12) for Hattie Major which is her fare to her home point, same being Mora, Washington. Please see that she leaves there with Amy Jackson as Amy is also bound for the same point or destination. Hattie's mother is now Mrs. Arthur Howeattle of the Quileute Reservation and she is to make her home with her mother. Her time is now up this year as she was there for a three-year term and the third year will elapse this school year which ends on the thirteenth instant at your school. Yours truly, H. T. Maskeshetewa, Teacher in Charge Quileute Indians. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., Jan.24, 1920 Mrs. Nicholson, Matron Cushman School Dear Mrs. Nicholson:- Please advise Hattie Major that she had no funds to her credit on the books at Taholah Agency and that the $5000 that Supt. Hill gave to her when she was home for Christmas vacation was advanced from his personal funds under the belief that she had some money to her credit. The Estate from which she eventually will receive some money has not yet been settled, hence the Superintendent cannot send her the money she requested. Very respectfully, Special Agent in Charge. OHX:MG 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE TAHOLAH INDIAN AGENCY, Taholah, Washington, December 15, 1918. Supt. E. S. Hammond, Cushman Trades School, Tacoma. Dear Sir: It has come to my notice that Lizzie Moses and Hattie Major are planning to come home for the holiday vacation. For reasons already given you, it is altogether better for these girls to be kept away from here as long as possible. Besides those reasons, I consider it inadvisable for them to come on account of the hazard of introducing influenza here. I have learned that Hattie has planned - with Lizzie's acquiescence in the plan- for her dead sister's husband, Mitchell Sam, with whom she corresponds, and a young married man, Charles Sampson, of Queets River, to come to Tacoma and there meet the girls. You can surmise the rest. I would like to suggest that if these fellows show up there you lay a trap for them and have them turned over to the police. No punishment you can give them will be half sufficient. Very truly yours, Otis B. Benson, Supt. Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash., Nov. 13, 1918. Dr. Otis O. Benson, Supt. Taholah, Washington. Dear Doctor: Replying to your of November 11th, I have had all correspondence to Lizzie Moses and Hattie Major carefully censured since your advice of last August and have intercepted and destroyed several "bad" letters. If any more arrive, I will forward them to the postal authorities for their action. These girls are obedient and modest in deportment and have given us no trouble so far. Next spring I shall endeavor for their sakes to retain them in school. If their parents stay away, I feel sure I can hold the girls. Addie Sam has had a serious attack of Spanish influenza and has been slow to recuperate. Last week she had several slight hemorrhages which were reported to our Doctor who advised me to allow Addie Sam to return home on leave of absence without delay. Addie left for home Monday, Nov. 11, 1918. Very respectfully, Superintendent DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR, U. S. INDIAN SERVICE. Form approved by the Comptroller of the Treasury February 1, 1908. THE CUSHMAN TRADES SCHOOL TACOMA, WASHINGTON. July 29th, 1918. Otis O. Benson. Superintendent & Physician. Taholah, Washington. Dear Mr. Benson: Hattie Major was allowed to return home for the vacation period on condition that she return promptly September 5th, to Cushman at her own expense. Hattie was a very good girl while at school and I very much regret hearing that she is suspected of such a trick. As the date for re-opening school is rapidly drawing near, I will appreciate any effort you may make to interest your children in Cushman, which is their home school. Owing to the excessive high price of printing this year, I have not sent out a prospectus of the school but assure you that the full, prescribed course from grades 1 thru 8 are given in the letter and the spirit. There are a number of boys in your jurisdiction who have been, or should be enrolled here. If you will kindly send me their names and addresses I shall be glad to write them personally. Very sincerely yours, Superintendent. 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE TAHOLA INDIAN AGENCY, Tahola, Wash., July 24, 1918. Supt. E. S. Hammond, Cushman Indian Agency, Tacoma, Wash. Dear Sir: A complaint has just reached me from the sister of Hattie Major on the alleged ground that the latter wrote a love-letter to the former's husband. When Hattie and her mother were in the office yesterday and I asked the girl about returning to your school, she gave me to understand that she was not intending to return. I would like to know what the understanding was between the mother and yourself when the girl was permitted to come home, whether she was to return. I will look further into the charge against her, and if there is a probability of guilt, I will have the Police at Quests River bring her in and I will return her at once. Very truly yours, Olex D. Turner, Supt. & Physician. Paholah Wash. Feb. 1, 1918 Dept. Cushman Ind. School Dear Sir, I have been wanting to write and inform you about the girls from Sweet River Lizzie Moses and Hettie Major. Their folks have very sore towards me because these girls had to come away to school. Mr. Dr. Keck worked hard to get these girls to school. I do all I can to help to get these girls come to school because I know it is for their own good. They can't learn at home but they made a lot of trouble now their folks want to get someone to marry them when they come home on vacation. Their folks are very foolish. They don't want them to come to school. I just want to let you know that they have bad name here up to Sweet. So you know what to do. I am yours truly, Albert Smith Ind Policeman RECORD OF PUPIL IN SCHOOL RECORD OF Hattie Major at Cushman Trade School. Takoma, Wash. This form must be executed in duplicate when a child is transferred from a reservation to a nonreservation school. The Superintendent of the nonreservation school will retain the original for his files, and the duplicate shall be deposited in the reservation school records. The reservation superintendent should send the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate as provided by law. All blank spaces must be properly filled in entirely in ink. If the information calls for an entry of "black" or "white," that fact should be stated. No space should be left unfilled. Whether the parents are living or dead, their names must be given. The person who signs the blank as consenting to the transfer should indicate his relation to the applicant by marking out the word "parent," "guardian," or "next of kin," leaving unmarked only the title appropriate to the signer. INDORSEMENTS. The laws relating to the transfer of Indian children from reservations and schools are as follows: That hereafter no Indian child shall be sent from any Indian reservation to a school beyond the State or Territory in which said reservation is situated without the voluntary consent of the father or mother of such child if either of them are living, and if neither of them are living without the voluntary consent of the next of kin of such child. Such consent shall be made before the agent of the reservation, and he shall send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate that such consent has been voluntarily given before such child shall be removed from such reservation. And it shall be unlawful for any Indian agent or other employee of the Government to induce, or seek to induce, by withholding rations or by other improper means, the parents or next of kin of any Indian to consent to the removal of any Indian child beyond the limits of any reservation. (28 Stats., p. 906.) Provided, That hereafter no Indian child shall be taken from any school in any State or Territory to a school in any other State against its will or without the written consent of its parents. (29 Stats., p. 348.) That no Indian pupil under the age of fourteen years shall be transported at Government expense to any Indian school beyond the limits of the State or Territory in which the parents of such child reside or of the adjoining State or Territory. (35 Stat. L., 781.) The rules provide that— A pupil who has been regularly enrolled in a nonreservation school must not be taken to any other nonreservation school without the consent of both superintendents and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and superintendents will be held to strict accountability for such pupils taken to their schools. An Indian boy or girl 18 years old and over may, without the consent of parents or others, personally sign the application form on its being changed to suit the case; but in all cases where the parents are living they should first be consulted.
